note: The nine proposed tasks, rewritten against Hugh's per-task feedback and all set in one invented project so no prompt reads as a test: a Python payments service at /home/user/checkout-api. Source: scratchpad proposed-prompts-v2.json. Nothing here was built when it was written; all nine have been built since. N10 is struck and gets no entry; the section header says so once.
section_note: Nine designs, all since built: the text here is each design as it was written, before any fixture or verifier existed, so the 'graded' sentences describe what a verifier was meant to assert rather than what the shipped one does. The tenth slot is unassigned — N10 was struck because requiring an interactive route is a method constraint and an R3 violation, and the proposal's own answer is to fill the slot from the survey's Tier 3 (2.1 split-by-path or 3.3 absorb-into-a-stack cover the salvageable ask, which is 'move exactly one hunk and leave the rest of the commit alone'). That slot was filled by a tenth new task, so the suite now stands at 24.
standing_constraints: Two rules were applied to every prompt: state every constraint the verifier scores and nothing it does not, and never name the technique, the subcommand or the flag.

tasks.headline: a conflict that propagates instead of being resolved on the spot
tasks.prompt: The rebase of retry-backoff onto main left src/client/retry.py conflicted in 'make the retry budget configurable', and everything above it is carrying the conflict too. Fix it in that commit — keep main's renamed REQUEST_TIMEOUT and my RETRY_BUDGET setting — and leave the stack as the four commits it is now, each with the changes it has.
tasks.design: **Setup:** retry-backoff's four commits have already been rebased onto a main that moved underneath them; the second of the four conflicts in src/client/retry.py because main renamed TIMEOUT in the same lines that commit added RETRY_BUDGET, and the two commits above it and the empty working copy all carry the propagated conflict. **Graded:** `conflicts()` empty across the whole repo, the four anchored change ids still resolving in the same order each carrying its own diff, no fifth commit between the anchored middle change and the anchored head, and retry.py at the head matching the single satisfying content line-wise. It discriminates the git-shaped model in which a conflict halts work and must be cleared before anything else happens — unpicking the stack commit by commit and landing a fixup on top both leave the anchored middle change conflicted.
tasks.open_question: Naming REQUEST_TIMEOUT and RETRY_BUDGET pins the resolution so it can be graded, but it tells the agent what the conflict contains before it looks.

tasks.headline: a merge commit the agent creates
tasks.prompt: I need rate-limit and oauth-refresh brought together: make a commit that sits on top of both, with config.toml carrying the [ratelimit] block from one and the [oauth] block from the other. Don't rewrite the commits on either bookmark.
tasks.design: **Setup:** rate-limit and oauth-refresh diverge from main, their tips edit the same region of config.toml so they conflict textually, and there is no merge anywhere in the repo. **Graded:** `@` has exactly two parents whose change ids are exactly the two anchored tips, the merge renders `conflict == false`, config.toml holds both named blocks at the one satisfying content, and both tips still resolve to their bootstrap commit ids — unchanged commit ids, not merely surviving change ids, which is what kills the hand-written single-parent union. It discriminates hunting for a `jj merge` subcommand from knowing that a commit can simply have two parents.
tasks.open_question: That there is no `jj merge` subcommand is marked 0.38-only in the provenance roster and has to be re-probed on 0.44 before authoring, since the whole discrimination assumes it.

tasks.headline: recovering from a mistake buried in the operation log
tasks.prompt: I squashed 'return 409 on duplicate keys' into 'add idempotency key to charge requests' by mistake, and I've made two more commits since then. Get those back to being two separate commits exactly as they were, without losing the work I did afterwards.
tasks.design: **Setup:** two commits above main that should have stayed apart, which the bootstrap has already squashed together, plus two further commits of real work made afterwards so the mistake is neither the first nor the last entry in the operation log. **Graded:** both anchored change ids visible again as separate commits in their original order, each carrying its own diff; the two later anchored changes still resolving with their bootstrap commit ids intact; an `--at-op` replay confirming the recovered commits are the originals rather than reconstructions; and every divergence addressed through `change_id(X)` rather than a bare change-id revset or the literal X/0, X/1 offsets. It discriminates undoing the most recent operation (which reverses the changelog commit) and rewinding to a pre-mistake operation (which reaches a repository missing the later work) from reversing one operation out of the middle of the history.
tasks.open_question: The correct route leaves a residual divergent change and legitimately drops a change id, so this will need an `anchor_exemptions.json` — and a green pre-sweep cannot reveal that it is missing, because the untouched image never does the work that breaks the assertion.
tasks.explainer_title: What this task sets up, and what it evaluates
explainer: **The setup.** The agent is handed a repository with a mistake already baked into it and some work done on top of the mistake. On top of main there were two commits — one adding an idempotency key to charge requests, one returning 409 when a duplicate key shows up — and the bootstrap squashed the second into the first, so the repository now holds a single commit carrying both changes and the second commit's message is gone. The bootstrap then made two more commits, a retry-budget change and a changelog entry, so the mistake sits three operations back rather than being the last thing that happened.
**A correct recovery** ends with those two commits separate again, carrying the same identities they had before the squash, and with the two later commits still present and unmodified.

**The obvious moves each fail in their own way.** Undoing the most recent operation reverses the changelog commit instead of the squash. Rewinding the repository to the state it was in before the squash also erases the two later commits, because that is time travel rather than an inverse patch. Hand-splitting the combined commit back into two produces commits that look right in a log but are new ones, which the verifier can tell apart from the originals.

**What is being evaluated** is whether the agent knows that jj's record of past operations lets you reverse one specific operation out of the middle of the history without disturbing what came after it — and, just as importantly, whether it can tell that apart from rewinding to an earlier point in time.

**Why it earns a slot.** This is precisely where the model most people carry over from git breaks: git's reflog lets you go back to a state, and an agent reasoning by analogy will reach for the equivalent here and quietly destroy a day of work. The cost is invisible from the end state — the repository looks perfectly fine, it just has less in it — which is exactly why it has to be graded rather than eyeballed.

tasks.headline: revsets the agent writes
tasks.prompt: get the change ids of all the tips not yet part of main and put them in unmerged.txt, each id on its own line
tasks.design: **Setup:** roughly sixteen commits across six lines of work — main, two already-landed bookmarks whose tips are ancestors of main, and four heads that are not — deliberately large and interleaved enough that reading the log and transcribing tips by eye is not a viable route. **Graded:** the reference revset is evaluated in the repo at verification time and unmerged.txt must equal that set of change ids exactly, so the expected answer never appears as a constant; every read passes `--ignore-working-copy` so the verifier does not snapshot what it is grading, and anchored ids confirm the history was not restructured to make a wrong answer true. Whether the agent composed a revset or worked it out by hand is not graded.
tasks.open_question: An answer-file task invites a zero-tool-call guess, so some fraction of trials measures agency rather than jj skill; the proposal prefers a form where the revset is the route to an action rather than the deliverable.

tasks.headline: filesets
tasks.prompt: roll back the src/ changes but don't change the generated tree
tasks.design: **Setup:** one commit, 'wire up the new charge client', touching both hand-written code under src/ and a regenerated tree nested under src/generated/, whose files carry machine-looking content with a recorded hash so they cannot be plausibly reconstructed — over-restoring and then re-adding them fails byte-equality. **Graded:** the anchored change's changed paths are exactly the generated set and nothing else, every file under src/generated/ matches the bootstrap byte for byte, and the change id survives the rewrite while the commit id changes, which is what distinguishes an in-place rewrite from a rebuilt commit. Doing it file by file also passes — the fileset is the cheap route, not the graded one. It discriminates a whole-directory restore, which silently takes the nested generated subtree with it.
tasks.open_question: No survey theme backs this one, so standing the fixture up and solving it on the pinned binary is the first authoring action rather than a later check.

tasks.headline: immutability
tasks.prompt: jj is refusing to reword anything in my stack — it says the commits are immutable — and 'fix nonce handling' should say 'fix nonce handling on retried charges'. Sort it out so I can rewrite my own commits again, and keep main and everything below it protected from rewrites.
tasks.recast_note: Recast to a single functional ask after the 'two unrelated tasks' objection: the standalone 'set the repo up so nothing can be rewritten' errand is gone, and the agent now enters on a refusal it has to diagnose. That is also the defence against the risk in the original — a prompt that opens by asking for protection reads like branch protection and pulls toward git-side mechanisms (hooks, `receive.denyNonFastForwards`, read-only files) that jj never reads.
tasks.design: **Setup:** main with two commits below it and a four-commit stack above, and an over-wide immutability alias the bootstrap has already configured through `jj config set --repo`, so the user's own stack is protected along with main and every rewrite in it is refused. **Graded:** the configured alias is evaluated in the repo and never string-matched — the anchored main change must still be inside it and the anchored stack commits must not — the anchored 'fix nonce handling' change carries the corrected description under the same change id with a new commit id, and the anchored commit below main is byte-identical to the bootstrap's. Both halves are scored, so narrowing the protection without doing the reword, and rewording while leaving main unprotected, each fail.
tasks.open_question: jj 0.44 silently accepts five config keys it removed — they exit 0, print nothing, list back happily and do nothing — so an agent that writes a plausible key sees no error and reports done. That is why the alias must be evaluated rather than read.

tasks.headline: the operation log as something you diagnose
tasks.prompt: Before I re-run the tests I need to know which commits actually changed when I rebased retry-backoff onto main — put their change ids in touched.txt, one per line.
tasks.design: **Setup:** an operation log holding one multi-commit rebase — retry-backoff's four commits moved onto an advanced main — among several small operations made afterwards, so the rebase is not the most recent entry and has to be found. **Graded:** the operation's effect is recomputed at verification time by `--at-op` differencing, reading the repo at the operation and at its predecessor and taking the change-id delta, and touched.txt is compared as a set; the expected set is never a constant, so a guessed list of plausible ids cannot match. It discriminates guessing the touched set from `jj log`, which shows the current graph rather than what the operation changed.
tasks.open_question: `--no-integrate-operation` and `jj op integrate` are real on 0.44, so an agent can produce side effects that leave no operation-log entry — which means a verifier reconstructing truth by `--at-op` differencing is reasoning over a log no longer guaranteed complete. The proposal wants this probed before N7 is authored.

tasks.headline: divergence as a thing to work with
tasks.prompt: jj is showing 'add idempotency key to charge requests' twice and the idempotency bookmark is in a conflicted state. Keep the copy that has tests/test_charge.py in it, get rid of the other, and leave idempotency pointing at the one that survives.
tasks.design: **Setup:** a bare origin alongside the repo; the change exists twice — the local side amended to also touch tests/test_charge.py, a colleague's rewrite of the same change fetched from the remote — so two visible commits share one change id and the idempotency bookmark is conflicted between the local and remote targets on the same log lines. **Graded:** exactly one commit matches `change_id(X)` and renders `divergent == false`, it is the side whose tree contains tests/test_charge.py, and the bookmark resolves unconflicted to it. Every revset must spell `change_id(X)` and `bookmarks(name)`, because a bare change-id revset errors on a divergent change and a bare bookmark name errors on a conflicted bookmark — this is a task whose own verifier is breakable by the exact trap it tests.
tasks.open_question: The solve legitimately drops a change id, so it needs an `anchor_exemptions.json` that a green pre-sweep cannot tell you is missing — and the list of operations that legitimately drop one was measured on 0.38 and never re-measured on 0.44.

tasks.headline: duplicate a range
tasks.prompt: The duplicate-key work — 'validate the idempotency key format' through 'add tests for duplicate keys' — needs to be on release/2.4 as well. Put copies of those commits there in the same order and leave the originals on main exactly where they are.
tasks.design: **Setup:** a release/2.4 maintenance line branching off main several commits back, and on main a contiguous run of three commits with unrelated commits both above and below it, so copying the wrong span is a detectably different end state. **Graded:** one new commit per source commit, each carrying exactly its source's diff, in source order, descending from the anchored release/2.4 tip; the duplicates are minted by the solve so they have no anchored ids and are located structurally and matched to sources by diff rather than by description; and both anchored originals must be intact — same change ids, same commit ids, same parents. It discriminates cherry-picking one commit at a time and, more sharply, the model in which 'get these over there' means a rebase, which relocates the originals instead of copying them.
tasks.open_question: `duplicate_commit`, the task this absorbs, is one of three known grader artifacts in the current suite and the cause has not been isolated; the replacement must not inherit it.
